newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Pemex pledges radical changes after disaster.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Pemex pledges radical changes after disaster.

text.p: Mexico's state oil company Petroleos Mexicanos on Thursday promised radical changes to improve safety following a deadly 36-hour fuel blaze this week just outside Mexico City.

Amid a storm of criticism over the fire, which killed four people, Pemex chairman Adrian Lajous said he planned to make the world's fifth largest oil company much safer to ensure accidents like this week's gasoline fire do not keep repeating themselves.

Disaster struck when Pemex workers were repairing a valve at a large gasoline storage tank facility on Monday. For an unknown reason, one of the tanks caught fire -- turning into a raging inferno that sent huge flames and a column of black smoke over North America's biggest city. It took hundreds of firemen nearly two days to put the fire out.

"I plan to present in the coming days to Pemex's board of directors a strategy, a series of radical steps that will allow us to improve safety at each and every Pemex facility, particularly those near urban areas," Lajous said in an interview with TV Azteca television network.
"There is no doubt in my mind we need to improve safety at Pemex," said Lajous, who has been the target of calls for his resignation by opposition lawmakers since the accident.
Lajous did not say what kinds of changes were in mind.

The state-owned oil firm is one of the world's biggest, producing about 2.85 million barrels of crude oil a day. It generates huge wealth for the Mexican government but critics say it has cut corners on safety.

Pemex has been struck by a series of disasters in recent years. Earlier this year, an explosion at a natural gas center killed six workers and started a huge fire that caused millions of dollars in damage.
And in 1992, gasoline from a Pemex facility leaked into the sewer system in Mexico's second city of Guadalajara and caused an explosion that blew apart entire avenues and killed more than 200 people.
